alternative: an explicit while/for loop with reassigned locals (or Iterator), java.util.stream reductions such as Stream.reduce for a collection fold, or a Deque-based work list / library trampoline for non-tail recursion
implementation_notes: The JVM offers no tail-call instruction and javac/HotSpot do not eliminate self-recursive tail calls, so a tail-recursive method keeps a frame per step and deep recursion ends in StackOverflowError - documented as thrown when an application recurses too deeply. Java's realization of the pattern is therefore its result: the accumulator becomes a local, the recursive call becomes an assignment inside a while/for loop, and collection accumulations move to java.util.stream reductions. Recursion stays appropriate only where depth is bounded by the data or by an explicitly enforced limit.
idiom_name: explicit while loop with accumulator locals (the JVM has no tail-call instruction)
pitfalls: StackOverflowError is an Error, and catching it is unreliable because the stack is already exhausted when it is thrown - bound the depth or convert to a loop.
Recursion inside a synchronized method holds the monitor per frame and delays cleanup; the eliminated-tail-call rewrite is also the fix for the lock-holding pattern.
Moving the loop into lambdas/Streams does not make it tail recursion - it hides the control flow - so keep reductions for folds and loops for state machines.
